|Former Honduran Chief of Staff linked to Colombian drug smuggling operations.<ref>{{cite news |id={{ProQuest|1894162289}} |title=Running A 'School For Dictators' |url=https://www.newsweek.com/running-school-dictators-192604 |work=Newsweek |date=8 August 1993 }}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Jesus A Marmol Yanes
|The Office of the Special Prosecutor for Human Rights accused Marmol Yanes of cover-up and abuse of authority in the killing of 15-year-old Ebed Jassiel Yanes Caceres in 2012<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-03-09 |title=Honduras |url=https://www.justice.gov/eoir/country/honduras-topical |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en |archive-date=April 2, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220402235702/https://www.justice.gov/eoir/country/honduras-topical |url-status=dead }}</ref> (2013 report).
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Juan Rubén Girón Reyes
|Was one of those charged with the cover up of Ebed Yanes’ death.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dictan medidas a oficiales acusados de encubrimiento |url=https://www.elheraldo.hn/sucesos/dictan-medidas-a-oficiales-acusados-de-encubrimiento-FJEH622502 |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=www.elheraldo.hn |language=es-HN}}</ref> According to one soldier they were ordered by Giron to pick up the shell casings and to not speak of what happened.<ref name="Arce">{{Cite web |last=Arce |first=Alberto |title=Dad seeks justice for son killed in broken Honduras |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2012/11/12/dad-seeks-justice-for-son-slain-in-broken-honduras/1699289/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=USA Today |language=en-US}}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Reynel Funes Ponce
|In 2013 he was accused of withholding information about the killing of Ebed Yanes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-02-22 |title=Renuncia subjefe de la Fuerzas Armadas de Honduras » Criterio.hn |url=https://criterio.hn/renuncia-subjefe-de-la-fuerzas-armadas-de-honduras/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=Criterio.hn |language=es}}</ref> He allegedly ordered that the weapons used in the incident be exchanged to cover up the killing.<ref name="Arce"/>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Herberth Bayardo Inestroza Membreño
|Denied that the forced removal of President Zelaya was a coup by saying “It was a fast operation. It was over in minutes, and there were no injuries, no deaths. We said, ‘Sir, we have a judicial order to detain you.’ We did it with respect.”<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lacey |first=Marc |date=2009-07-01 |title=Leader's Ouster Not a Coup, Says the Honduran Military |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/07/02/world/americas/02coup.html |access-date=2022-04-02 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Later he admitted to the Miami Herald that the act of removing Zelaya from the country went beyond the scope of the judicial order. "In the moment that we took him out of the country, in the way that he was taken out, there is a crime. Because of the circumstances of the moment this crime occurred, there is going to be a justification and cause for acquittal that will protect us."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2009-07-08 |title=Top Honduran military lawyer: We broke the law – Diario Judío México |url=https://diariojudio.com/noticias/internacionales/top-honduran-military-lawyer-we-broke-the-law/79470/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=Diario Judío: Diario de la Vida Judía en México y el Mundo |language=es}}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Luis Javier Prince Suazo
|During the 2009 coup as head of the [[Honduran Air Force]] he arranged for President Zelaya to be flown into exile<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-03-30 |title=One year after Cáceres murder, US ties to Honduras endure, killings continue |url=https://www.ncronline.org/news/justice/one-year-after-caceres-murder-us-ties-honduras-endure-killings-continue |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=National Catholic Reporter |language=en}}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Honduras}}
|Gustavo Alvarez Martínez
|A 1997 CIA study identified the Honduran Anti-Communist Liberation Army, or ELACH, as a "death squad" with close ties to a special security unit reporting to Alvarez. In 1983, a dissident [[Honduran Army]] officer accused Alvarez of masterminding "death squads." In 1994 a lawyer appointed by the Honduran parliament to investigate human rights abuse blamed the Honduran army for 174 disappearances and kidnappings in the 1980s. Most of the incidents took place before the 1984 ouster of Alvarez. In 1984 Alvarez was accused by his fellow generals of abuse of power and sent into exile.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2011-06-29 |title=washingtonpost.com: Negroponte's Time In Honduras at Issue |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=http://www.washingtonpost.com/ac2/wp-dyn/A52001-2005Mar20?language=printer |access-date=2022-04-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629054237/http://www.washingtonpost.com/ac2/wp-dyn/A52001-2005Mar20?language=printer |archive-date=June 29, 2011 }}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Mexico}}
|''[[Los Zetas]]''
|Though the Mexican and US Governments have never released a full list, several sources claimed that many of the initial 34 founders of Los Zetas were [[GAFE]] Special Forces Operators trained at SOA throughout the late 80s to early 90s.<ref name=":12b">{{cite web|url=http://www.soaw.org/component/content/article/1/1994|title=U.S.-trained ex-soldiers form core of "Zetas" - SOA Watch: Close the School of the Americas|last=Udu-gama|first=Nico|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170418211956/http://www.soaw.org/component/content/article/1/1994|archive-date=2017-04-18 |access-date=November 27, 2016}}</ref><ref name=":13">{{cite web|url=http://www.cronica.com.mx/notas/2004/158801.html|title=Los Zetas fueron entrenados por la Escuela de las Américas|date=December 20, 2004|work=La Crónica de Hoy|language=es |access-date=January 31, 2019|archive-date=February 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225134251/http://www.cronica.com.mx/notas/2004/158801.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Panama}}
|[[Omar Torrijos]]
|Commander of the Panamanian [[Military of Panama|National Guard]] and the ''[[de facto]]'' dictator of [[Panama]] from 1968 to 1981. Torrijos was never officially the [[List of heads of state of Panama|president of Panama]], but instead held titles including "Leader of the Panamanian Revolution" and "Chief of Government." Torrijos took power in a ''[[coup d'état]]'' and instituted a number of social reforms.
|-
|{{flagcountry|Panama}}
|[[Manuel Noriega]]
|Panamanian politician and military officer who was the ''[[de facto]]'' ruler of [[Panama]] from 1983 to 1989. He had longstanding ties to United States intelligence agencies; however, he was removed from power by the [[United States invasion of Panama|U.S. invasion of Panama]].
|-
|{{flagcountry|Peru}}
|[[Juan Velasco Alvarado]]
|[[Left-wing politics|Left-wing]] Peruvian General who served as the 58th [[President of Peru]] during the dictatorship from 1968 to 1975<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://elpais.com/diario/1984/08/19/internacional/461714415_850215.html|title=Estados Unidos anuncia el cierre de la Escuela de las Américas, en la que se han graduado 44.000 militares latinoamericanos|newspaper=El País |date=August 18, 1984|via=elpais.com}}</ref>
|-
|{{flagcountry|Peru}}
|[[Vladimiro Montesinos]]
|Former long-standing head of [[Peru]]'s [[Intelligence (information gathering)|intelligence]] service, [[National Intelligence Service (Peru)|Servicio de Inteligencia Nacional]] (SIN), under [[President of Peru|President]] [[Alberto Fujimori]].
|-
|{{flagcountry|Peru}}
|[[Ollanta Humala]]
|[[Peru]]vian politician who served as the 65th [[President of Peru]] from 2011 to 2016.
|-
|{{flagcountry|Venezuela}}
|[[Vladimir Padrino López]]
|[[Ministry of Defense (Venezuela)|Minister of Defense]] for the [[National Armed Forces of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela]] under [[Nicolás Maduro]]. Sanctioned by the United States for human rights abuses against opposition protesters and dissidents, corruption leading to the economic collapse of the country, and drug trafficking charges. Attended [[Psychological operations (United States)|psychological operations]] courses at SOA in 1995.
|-
|{{flagcountry|Venezuela}}
|[[Gustavo González López]]
|Venezuelan [[Ministry of Popular Power for Interior, Justice and Peace|Minister of Popular Power for Interior, Justice and Peace]] (MPPRIJP) from 2015 to 2016. Current director of the National Intelligence Service (SEBIN). Sanctioned by the United States for human rights abuses against opposition protesters and dissidents, corruption leading to the economic collapse of the country, and drug trafficking charges. Attended [[Psychological operations (United States)|psychological operations]] courses at SOA in 1991.
|-
|{{flagcountry|Venezuela}}
|[[Nestor Reverol]]
|Venezuelan [[Ministry of Popular Power for Interior, Justice and Peace|Minister of Popular Power for Interior, Justice and Peace]]. Former Commander of the [[Venezuelan National Guard]] (BNG) from 2014 to 2016. Responsible for killings and torture of Protesters during his tenure as BNG Commander. Sanctioned by the United States for human rights abuses against opposition protesters and dissidents, corruption leading to the economic collapse of the country, and drug trafficking charges. Attended [[Psychological operations (United States)|psychological operations]] courses at SOA in 1996.<ref>{{cite news|title=Exclusive: U.S. to charge Venezuela's National Guard chief with drug trafficking|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-venezuela-usa-idUSKBN0TY2RV20151216|access-date=12 April 2017|work=[[Reuters]]|date=16 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Exclusive: U.S. to charge Venezuela's National Guard chief with drug trafficking|url=https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/democraciaabierta/chavistas-escuela-de-las-americas-en/|access-date=12 April 2017|work=Open Democracy|date=22 October 2020}}</ref>
|}

==Media representation==

* ''[[School of the Americas Assassins]]'', a 1994 short documentary film produced by [[Robert Richter (American film producer)|Robert Richter]]. It was nominated for an [[Academy Award]] for [[Academy Award for Best Documentary (Short Subject)|Best Documentary Short]]
* ''{{visible anchor|Hidden in Plain Sight}}'',<ref>{{IMDb title|0384994|Hidden in Plain Sight}}</ref> a 2003 feature-length documentary film produced by Andrés Thomas Conteris, Vivi Letsou, and John Smihula
* ''[[The War on Democracy]]'', a 2007 documentary film produced by Youngheart Entertainment PTY Limited
* ''{{visible anchor|The Empire Files: The U.S. School That Trains Dictators and Death Squads}}'', a 2015 documentary produced by [[Abby Martin]] and broadcast on [[Telesur (TV channel)|teleSUR]]
* ''[[El Conde (film)|El Conde]]'', a 2023 Chilean fictional film by Pablo Larrain
